BY DAVID B. WILLSON.
It has been deemed well to supplement the foregoing
sketch of Beta Beta, and the facts mentioned incidentally
in the communications elsewhere, by stating briefly one
or two things as yet unnoticed, and the steps taken
to enter Psi Upsilon.
Throughout its whole career the Order of Beta Beta
was
distinguished by the active and continued interest of
the graduate members in all its concerns.
This, besides
the common tie of friendship and the mutual pride in
its acknowledged reputation for excellence of scholar
ship, was due chiefly to the fact, that two annual festi
vals were
always held- -one in February, for the ad
mission of new members, and one at Commencement�
to
which every member was formally invited, and was
privi
leged to share in the deUberations on all general
questions. No thought had ever been entertained of
uniting with any other society.
The movement for union with Psi Upsilon arose unex
pectedly and was carried along with singular rapidity
and remarkable unanimity. The first suggestions came
from the Rev. A. B. Crawford, Zeta, '76, then a student
in the Berkeley Divinity School, Middletown, Conn., in
conversation with some of his fellow students who were
Beta Betas. No encouragement was
given him at the
time and few of the members of the Order heard of it.
It, however, becoming known in March, 1879, to some of
the active menibers, who had been noting with much care
the changes taking place in undergraduate Ufe at
Trinity,
they were convinced that the time had come for Beta
Beta, while yet in fuU strength and vigor, to make such
.
changes as would ensure her continued prosperity and en
large her sympathies.
A meeting was called March 31, when after a free iuterchange of views, the'' whole subject of affiUation with a
chaptered society was referred to a committee of three
active members, Bros. Willson, Crosby and Carpenter, to
make inquiries, and report whether, in their opinion, the
step was advisable.
The committee, besides communicating with a number
of graduate members of the Order, informally conferred
with Bro. Crawford, who, in the meantime (having pre
viously been addressed) had been invited by Mr. C. W.
Smiley, Secretary of the Executive Council of Psi Upsilon,
in his behalf, to acquaint himself of the present condi
tion and past history of Beta Beta. They afterwards met
a special committee of Psi Upsilon at New Haven, May
6th, at the time of its General Convention, consisting
of Bros. Wright, Beta, '42, Robinson, Beta, '41, Bangs,
Lambda, '78, Lobdell, Gamma, '58, and Warren, Xi, '80.
Through these interviews the plan of having the question
referred to a joint committee from both bodies clothed
with fuU powers to approve or disapprove, and to
arrange terms of agreement, for the purpose of faciMtating
negotiations, was decided upon; provided, of course, the
whole project would be approved by Psi Upsilon in its
general convention, and by the Order of Beta Beta at its
Commencement festival in June.
The active members of Beta Beta, being assured of the
the friendliness of Psi Upsilon by the appointment of the
committee suggested, and having decided by a unanimous
vote that the step was expedient and wise, directed the
same committee to prepare an address embodying their
views to be sent to the graduate members, without whose
approval and consent it was felt the union could not be
made, and which had been so stated in all iuterviews with
the representatives of Psi Upsilon. The reason was ob
vious. Beta Beta wished to retain, as a
chapter, all the
strength she had possessed as a local body and this could
only be secured by preser'ving her membership intact.
The subjoined circular letter was therefore sent out

Since addressing you a few weeks ago, the idea of
affiliation with a chaptered society was suggested to. the

was more

was with much sorrow that we came to this conclusion,

The necessity of the step being evident, the present
strength of the Order is a reason for the change being
made immediately, as it will enable us to effect a union
with the best organization now unrepresented at Trinity.
Were it to be deferred until the Order had deteriorated
the opportunity for cTwice would be gone, and none but an
inferior body would be willing to receive us. A favorable
opportunity for affiliation with the Psi Upsilon, a frater
nity possessing the highest reputation for scholarship,
social position and character, is now offered. Shall we
accept it? Such is the question which must be decided at

subject being so
large, we cannot here enter into a full
discussion of it, nor, perhaps, would it at all be necessary
or proper. We would ask, however, your earnest con
sideration of the following facts, which go to show the
sitiiation in which we are
placed, the sentiment against
which we have to battle, and the principal changes in

At Trinity, there were three local societies (I. K. A.,
Phi Kappa and Beta Beta), and about 1851 a chapter
society was estabUshed, the Delta Psi. Now, there are
three strong chaptered societies (Delta Psi, Alpha Delta
Phi and Delta Kappa Epsilon) and only two local societies
(Beta Beta and I. K. A.) The I. K. A., we have posi
tive information, has applied for admittance to a
Chap
tered Society.
From experience in electioneering, observation and in
quiry we find that there is a decided preference for chap
tered societies among young men coming to college.
Many of the best men, and the majority of all who can
come here, are pledged beforehand through the instru
mentality of other chapters or their graduate members.
It has been asked�
"Why cannot Bsta Beta occupy
the place here which the Skull and Bones, and Scroll and
Key societies hold at Yale?"
The small number of undergraduates at Trinity and the
transmitted society feehng which exists, prevent Beta Beta
from assuming such a position. Skull and Bones, and
Scroll and Key are senior societies, and admit members
without respect to chapter or class fraternities ; we, like
the others here, are full course societies.
The change, if made, wiU not effect the objects of Beta
Beta. It wfll only touch her outward form. Most of her
old customs may be kept. The traditions of the Order
will still survive. Her principles will remain unchanged.
Her name would be retained. All the brethren would,
of course, be continued in membership.
A new badge would be necessary, but the essentials of
Beta Beta's could be made the chapter pin.
In closing, we dall your attention also to the opinion of
two of our most esteemed brethren. A full and detailed
report will be made at our Commencement festival, by a
special committee to whom the subject has been referred. It
is hoped that as many of the brethren as possible will^ndeavor to be present.
We remain.

Convention Records.
From 1841 to the present time, with the possible excep
tion of the year 1842, annual Conventions of the frater
nity have been appointed. The conventions have been
held every year, except in 1862, when there was no
quorum present. There have been, thus far, either 37 or
38 General Conventions. The records of these conventions
constitute the only complete history of the progress of the
fraternity, the modifications in its constitution and laws,
as well as the estabhshment of new
chapters from time to
time. They are thus of the greatest importance, and yet
the copies are surprisingly few. It would be supposed
that each chapter would," as a matter of course, have com
plete sets since its organization. In response to the ques
tion as to how many copies are in each chapter, returns
have been received from all the chapters, and the follow
ing table contains the results. That some
steps should
be taken to preserve copies of all these, or to compile and
print an epitomized edition is too plain to need argument.
The proper body wiU, it may be hoped, take such steps
at its earliest opportunity.
The manuscript series extends from 1841 to 1871 inclu
sive ; the printed series from 1872 to date.
